title: Chapter 64 — Stubb’s Supper
paragraphs: Stubb's whale had been killed some distance from the ship. It was calm, so forming a tandem of three boats, we began the slow business of towing the prize back to the Pequod. And now, as we eighteen men with our thirty-six arms and one hundred eighty thumbs and fingers slowly toiled hour after hour upon that lifeless, sluggish corpse in the sea — and it seemed hardly to budge at all, except at long intervals — bitter, impatient thoughts began to fill us about the good old owner of the sea, and his way of keeping things. It was a funeral procession, and we were the pallbearers.

Darkness came on, but three lights up and down in the Pequod's main-rigging dimly guided our way, until drawing nearer we saw Ahab lowering one of several more lanterns over the bulwarks. Gazing blankly at the heaving whale for a moment, he issued the usual orders for securing it for the night, then handed his lantern to a seaman and went his way into the darkness, muttering to himself.

Though, in overseeing the pursuit of this whale, Captain Ahab had shown his customary energy — to call it that — now that the creature was dead, some vague dissatisfaction, or impatience, or despair, seemed to be working in him. As if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was yet to be killed, and though a thousand other whales were brought alongside, not one could be Moby Dick. And that hateful, incurable itch that tells a man he is not where he should be — that itch must have been eating at him.

A small note may as well be added here. The strongest and most reliable hold which the ship has upon the whale when moored alongside is by the flukes or tail. And since from its greater density that part is relatively heavier than any other — except the side-fins — its flexibility, even in death, causes it to sink low beneath the surface. So that a strong chain must be used to secure it. The chain is passed through the natural indentation at the narrowest part of the tail, near its base. This arrangement, however, does not prevent the tail from dropping completely below the surface at times.

If moody Ahab was now all quiet — at least as far as could be seen on deck — Stubb, his second mate, flushed with conquest, showed an unusual but still good-natured excitement. He was in such a bustle that the sober Starbuck, his official superior, quietly handed over to him the sole management of affairs. One small helpful task from Starbuck was readily accepted by Stubb.
"A steak, a steak, before I sleep! You, Daggoo! Overboard you go, and cut me one from his flank!"

Here be it known that though these wild fishermen do not, as a general thing and in keeping with the great military maxim, make the enemy pay for the war expenses — at least not before cashing in on the voyage's profits — yet now and then you find some of these Nantucketers who have a genuine taste for that particular part of the Sperm Whale known as the whale steak. It is a thick, firm slab cut from the tapering part of the body just behind the side-fin.

Around midnight that steak was cut and cooked. Lit by two lanterns of sperm oil, Stubb firmly stood up to his spermaceti supper at the capstan-head, as if that capstan were a sideboard. Nor was Stubb the only diner on whale flesh that night. Mingling their munchings with his own, thousands upon thousands of sharks, swarming around the dead whale, were feasting on his fat. A few sleepers below in their bunks were often startled by the sharp slapping of their tails against the hull, within a few inches of the sleepers' hearts. Looking over the side, you could just see them — as you might at night see the shining of silver in a graveyard — wallowing in the black waters, turning over on their backs as they scooped out huge mouthfuls of whale flesh, so that you could see their wide gaping mouths and the brightness of their teeth gleaming in the moonlight.

Though amid all the smoking horror and devilry of a sea-fight, sharks will be seen longingly gazing up at the ship's decks, like hungry dogs around a table where red meat is being carved, ready to gulp down every killed man tossed to them — and though while the brave butchers above deck are thus cannibally carving each other's live flesh with their swords and cutlasses, the sharks below should all the while be surgically cutting away under the very table at which the butchers are eating — though all this is appalling, it is even worse to consider that the same sharks have been known to snap at the oars of the whaleboats. Yes, sometimes they would bite off pieces of the blades themselves. Such were the sharks that fed around Stubb's whale that night.
But as yet Stubb paid no attention to the feast being held so close to him, any more than the sharks noticed the smacking of his own gourmet lips.

"Cook, cook! — where's that old Fleece?" he cried at length, spreading his legs still wider as if to form a more secure base for his supper, and at the same time stabbing his fork into the dish as if it were a lance. "Cook, you cook! — sail this way, cook!"

The old black man, not at all pleased about having been previously roused from his warm hammock at a most unreasonable hour, came shuffling along from his galley. For like many old black men, there was something the matter with his knees, which he did not keep well oiled like his other pans. This old Fleece, as they called him, came shambling up to the capstan. His left hand held a lantern, and in his right a long cooking fork with which he occasionally rapped his limping knee as a horseman raps his riding boot.

"Cook," said Stubb, quickly lifting a rather reddish piece to his mouth, "don't you think this steak is rather overdone? You've been beating this steak too much, cook. It's too tender. Don't I always say that to be good, a whale steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side — don't you see they prefer it tough and rare? What a racket they're making! Cook, go and talk to them. Tell them they are welcome to help themselves civilly, and in moderation, but they must keep quiet. Blast me if I can hear my own voice. Away, cook, and deliver my message. There, take this lantern — now go and preach to them!"

Sullenly taking the offered lantern, old Fleece limped across the deck to the bulwarks. Then, with one hand dangling his light low over the sea to get a good view of his congregation, with the other hand he solemnly brandished his cooking fork, and leaning far over the side, in a mumbling voice began addressing the sharks, while Stubb, softly crawling behind, listened to what he had to say.

"Fellow creatures: I've been ordered here to say that you must stop that damn noise down there. You hear? Stop that damn smacking of your lips! Mr. Stubb says that you can fill your damn bellies up to the hatches, but by God, you must stop that damn racket!"
"Cook," Stubb cut in, slapping him on the shoulder, "Cook! Why, damn your eyes, you mustn't swear that way when you're preaching. That's no way to convert sinners, cook!"
"Who's that? Then preach to them yourself," he replied sullenly, turning to go.
"No, cook. Go on, go on."
"Well, then — beloved fellow creatures —"
"Right!" exclaimed Stubb approvingly. "Coax them into it. Try that." And Fleece continued.

"You is all sharks, and by nature very voracious. Yet I say to you, fellow creatures, that that voraciousness — stop that damn slapping of your tails! How do you think you can hear, if you keep up such a damn slapping and biting down there?"
"Cook," cried Stubb, grabbing him by the collar, "I won't have that swearing. Talk to them like gentlemen."
Once more the sermon proceeded.

"Your voraciousness, fellow creatures, I don't blame you so much for. That is nature, and can't be helped. But to govern that wicked nature, that is the point. You is sharks, for certain. But if you govern the shark in you, why then you'd be an angel. For all an angel is, is nothing more than the shark well governed. Now, look here, brothers, just try once to be civil, a helping hand to each other — a little charity between yourselves — don't be grabbing all you can, and starving the rest of the neighborhood. I know you're very hungry right now. But, fellow creatures, just think about it — can you really be filling your bellies when your neighbor's belly is empty? And is it really good behavior to be knocking each other about like that? If you're going to eat, eat peaceful-like. There's room enough for everyone."
"Well done, old Fleece!" cried Stubb. "That's Christianity. Go on."

"No use going on. The damn villains will keep on squabbling and slapping each other, Mr. Stubb. They don't hear a word. No use preaching to such damn gluttons as you call them, till their bellies is full. And their bellies is bottomless. And when they do get them full, they won't hear you then either, for then they sink in the sea, go fast asleep on the coral, and can't hear nothing at all."
"Upon my soul, I am about of the same opinion. So give the benediction, Fleece, and I'll get back to my supper."
Upon this, Fleece, holding both hands over the fishy mob, raised his shrill voice and cried —
"Cursed fellow creatures! Kick up the damnedest row you can! Fill your damn bellies till they burst — and then die."
"Now, cook," said Stubb, resuming his supper at the capstan, "stand just where you stood before, there, across from me, and pay particular attention."
"All attention," said Fleece, again stooping over on his fork in the desired position.
"Well," said Stubb, helping himself generously meanwhile, "I shall now go back to the subject of this steak. In the first place, how old are you, cook?"
"What's that got to do with the steak?" said the old black man, testily.
"Silence! How old are you, cook?"
"About ninety, they say," he muttered gloomily.

"And you have lived in this world close to one hundred years, cook, and don't know yet how to cook a whale steak?" — rapidly swallowing another mouthful at the last word, so that it seemed a continuation of the question. "Where were you born, cook?"
"Behind the hatchway, on a ferryboat, going over the Roanoke."
"Born on a ferryboat! That's odd, too. But I want to know what country you were born in, cook!"
"Didn't I say the Roanoke country?" he cried sharply.
"No, you didn't, cook. But I'll tell you what I'm getting at, cook. You must go home and be born all over again. You don't know how to cook a whale steak yet."
"Bless my soul, if I cook another one," he growled angrily, turning around to leave.

"Come back, cook — here, hand me those tongs — now take that bit of steak there, and tell me if you think that steak is cooked as it should be? Take it, I say" — holding the tongs toward him — "take it, and taste it."
Faintly smacking his withered lips over it for a moment, the old man muttered, "Best cooked steak I ever tasted. Juicy, very juicy."
"Cook," said Stubb, squaring himself once more, "do you belong to the church?"
"Passed one once in Cape Town," said the old man sullenly.

"And you have once in your life passed a holy church in Cape Town, where you no doubt overheard a holy parson addressing his listeners as his beloved fellow-creatures — have you, cook! And yet you come here and tell me such a dreadful lie as you just did, eh?" said Stubb. "Where do you expect to go, cook?"
"Go to bed very soon," he mumbled, half-turning as he spoke.
"Halt! Heave to! I mean when you die, cook. It's an awful question. Now what's your answer?"
"When this old black man dies," said the cook slowly, changing his whole manner and tone, "he himself won't go nowhere. But some blessed angel will come and fetch him."
"Fetch him? How? In a coach and four, as they fetched Elijah? And fetch him where?"
"Up there," said Fleece, holding his tongs straight over his head and keeping them there very solemnly.
"So then, you expect to go up into our main-top, do you, cook, when you are dead? But don't you know the higher you climb, the colder it gets? Main-top, eh?"
"Didn't say that at all," said Fleece, sulking again.

"You said up there, didn't you? And now look where your tongs are pointing. But perhaps you expect to get into heaven by crawling through the lubber's hole, cook. But no, no, cook — you don't get there except you go the regular way, round by the rigging. It's a tricky business, but must be done, or else it's a no-go. But none of us are in heaven yet. Drop your tongs, cook — listen, now. Look here, cook — you expect to go to heaven — turn your face around — do you expect to go to heaven, cook? Answer me!"
"All attention," said the old black man, placing both hands as requested, vainly wriggling his grizzled head as if trying to get both ears pointed forward at the same time.

"Well then, cook — you see this whale steak of yours was so very bad that I have put it out of sight as soon as possible. You see that, don't you? Well, for the future, when you cook another whale steak for my private table here at the capstan, I'll tell you what to do so as not to spoil it by overdoing. Hold the steak in one hand, and show a live coal to it with the other. That done, dish it. Do you hear? And now, tomorrow night, you will cook another steak for me — and now get to bed."
But Fleece had hardly gotten three steps away when he was called back.
"Cook, give me cutlets for supper tomorrow night during the mid-watch. Do you hear? Away you sail, then. — Wait! Stop! Take a bow before you go. — Hold on! Whale-balls for breakfast — don't forget."

"Wish to God the whale had eaten him instead of him eating the whale. I'm blessed if he ain't more of a shark than the sharks themselves," muttered the old man, limping away. With which wise remark he went to his hammock.
